en: The duty to inform, under the CDC regime, is not satisfied by the mere formal existence of content available to the consumer. In the case of immaterial objects of consumption, information fulfills its legal function only when it organizes, in an intelligible and timely manner, the practical core of the decision. This means that informing is not dumping clauses, FAQs, hyperlinks, peripheral notices and cascading policies only to invoke formal compliance afterwards. Informing is making cognizable, at the point of decision, what actually defines the utility of the performance, its risks, its relevant limits, its conditions of enjoyment and the cases in which it may be lost. The consumer-law system requires, in material terms, that the supplier ensure the consumer clear, precise and conspicuous information about the main characteristics of the product, its economic repercussions and the risks that surround the contracting, so that good faith and trust are not sabotaged by a documentary architecture that delivers words and withholds meaning<1><2>707</2></1>.

<1>p. 619</1> This requirement is especially important in IOCs because the essential content of the relationship is not in peripheral details, but in the very core of the value acquired. Real cost, total cost, mutability of the object, restrictions on use, equivalence parameters, maintenance criteria, cases of loss and consequences of acceptance are not exotic annexes to the contracting. They are the substance of the promised enjoyment. When these elements appear displaced to zones of low visibility, scattered across secondary documents or subordinated to successive cross-references, the duty to inform has not been fulfilled in the material sense, even if the supplier manages to point to dozens of screens, links or supposedly accessible texts. The legal problem ceases to be the simple lack of information and becomes the communicational inadequacy of the supply.

Thus, the interpretive key is not quantity, but adequacy. The supplier does not fulfill the legal duty by accumulating documentation and leaving it technically available. Fulfillment is measured by the capacity of the information to reach the consumer in conditions that can actually guide a decision. The posture required is not passive. The supplier must make the information reach the recipient in a useful and structured way, because the consumer's right to information is a more complex problem than the mere lack of data to be provided<1><2>708</2></1>. This point is decisive. The standard defense that “it was all in the terms” only works if one accepts, uncritically, that the mere existence of a body of documents suffices to form valid consent. The CDC does not work with this fiction, so comfortable for the supplier.

From this follows the need to recognize that informational excess can also be a form of violation. Volume is not neutral. In certain communicational designs, it operates as a positive technique of opacity. The information exists, but its organization makes practical understanding of what matters unfeasible. Successive layers of documents, serialized links, cross-references, excessively technical language, inverted visual emphasis, cascading <1>disclaimers</1> and the displacement of relevant content to improbable zones of the contracting flow can produce the same legal effect as omission. The consumer receives text, <2>p. 620</2> but does not receive guidance. The platform stages informational openness while maintaining, under an appearance of compliance, a regime of noise. This is exactly the phenomenon called “performative transparency”.

Performative transparency does not consist in the absence of information, but in the excess, dispersion and defective hierarchization of the essential content. The supplier appears to fulfill the legal duty through abundance, but the communicational design reduces the practical utility of what it presents. This is not a mere aesthetic deficiency of drafting or a discomfort of reading. It is a structure that prevents comparison, understanding of the risk and apprehension of the economic and functional core of the contracting. In a consumer-law key, this failure is legally relevant because it compromises the practical freedom of choice. If the communication reduces price transparency, hinders the comparability of offers and materially interferes with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms, costs and conditions of the product or service, documentary abundance no longer functions as proof of transparency, but as its caricature<1><2>709</2></1>.

This point gains special density in IOCs because enjoyment is usually preceded by purchase and acceptance flows designed for speed, impulse, managed scarcity or a promise of distinction. In such environments, displacing the essential content outside the point of decision is more than a failure of organization. It is a shielding technique. The platform offers the object under a certain frame of value and urgency, but places costs, mutability, potential losses and limitations in documentary zones that the flow itself does not encourage one to go through. The consumer is pushed to decide on the basis of the shop window and only later discovers, if at all, the depth of the contractual reservation against their own enjoyment. The legally relevant question, then, is not whether there was text somewhere in the ecosystem. The question is whether the essential was presented in a conspicuous, legible and timely way before adhesion and before exposure to the risk.

<1>p. 621</1> This is precisely what Article 54, under paragraphs 3 and 4, of the CDC makes explicit. Adhesion contracts must be drafted in clear terms, with conspicuous and legible characters, so as to facilitate their understanding, and clauses limiting rights must be drafted with emphasis, allowing immediate and easy understanding<2><3>710</3></2>. The provision is not a typographical whim. It prevents the essential from being hidden in cross-references, low visibility or documentary depth. In IOCs, this command carries even greater weight, because a large part of the relevant limitations falls precisely on the core of the acquired experience. If the platform intends to reserve for itself the power to alter equivalence parameters, reduce functionality, condition the permanence of content, suppress access or redistribute risks, it cannot bury this under textual mountains and then claim that the consumer was informed in advance.

From this perspective, adequate information is that which presents the essential at the moment the consumer needs to decide. Its criterion is neither merely formal nor merely semantic. It is functional. Information must allow use, comparison and concrete evaluation of the performance before adhesion. In practical terms, this means that the informational regime must clearly expose, at the point of decision, the elements that structure the choice: price, total cost, relevant restrictions, ordinary mutability of the object, equivalence criteria, potential loss of items, refund conditions, cases of suspension, limits of use and substantial impacts of updates. When this content is only revealed through later investigation in long documents, consent is already born under a deficit of intelligibility. Adequate information is not that which exists in some remote corner of the system. It is that which arrives in time and with practical utility for deliberation<1><2>711</2></1>.

This shift of focus, from the existence of information to its adequacy, neutralizes the supplier's main alibi in platformized markets. The typical defense maintains that the consumer could have read everything calmly, simply by clicking more, opening more links, following more <1>p. 622</1> cross-references or consulting FAQs and complementary policies. The problem with this defense is that it turns the duty to inform into an obligation of documentary treasure hunting on the part of the consumer. The CDC does not admit this. The protection of trust and good faith prevent the supplier from treating engineered obscurity as proof of contractual freedom. No average consumer can be considered fully informed merely because, in theory, it was possible for them to go through a documentary forest, decode technical vocabulary and reconstruct on their own the hierarchy of what was really essential. When the documentary architecture demands this kind of pilgrimage, transparency has already failed.

For this reason too, excessive cross-references, opaque chains and overly long texts are not legally innocent. The mere mention that certain general conditions exist is not enough to include them validly in the relationship. The consumer must be able actually to read and understand what the clauses mean, which rights they limit and which obligations they create. Furtive texts, an excess of cross-references, dense language and hostile graphic materiality compromise the intelligibility of the essential content and, consequently, the very legitimacy of adhesion<1><2>712</2></1>. Obscurity, here, is not a regrettable stylistic detail. It is a way of organizing contractual risk for the benefit of the dominant party.

The notion of performative transparency is useful precisely because it captures this difference between formal existence and decisional utility. There is performative transparency when the supplier can demonstrate informational abundance, but cannot demonstrate that the essential core was presented in a clear, conspicuous and functionally guiding way. The performance of compliance replaces the effectiveness of the duty. The system comes to produce proof of formal coverage of the supplier's risk, not of the consumer's enlightenment. On platforms, this is especially visible when purchase screens emphasize urgency, rarity, bonuses, convenience or distinction and reserve the relevant conditions for contractual depth. The contract ceases to be an instrument of information and becomes a piece of ex post shielding.

<1>p. 623</1> The dogmatic consequence is important. If excess, noise and performative transparency can constitute a violation of the duty to inform, legal control cannot be limited to an abstract reading of the contract. It is necessary to reconstruct the concrete form in which the information was displayed, the moment it appeared, the interface that conveyed it, the emphasis it effectively received and the position it occupied in the decision path. In IOCs, proof of informational adequacy depends on minimum documentation of the purchase flow, the confirmation screens, the change notices, the way equivalences are presented and the visual location of the relevant limitations. It is not enough for the platform to claim generically that it informed. It must be in a position to demonstrate how it informed, when it informed and with what emphasis it informed.

It is here that the bridge to auditability is prepared. The transparency required by the CDC, in a governed environment, cannot merely be declared. It must be verifiable. This involves minimum preservation of interface trails, version history of screens, relevant messages, change notices and documentation of the communicational design actually employed. When the proof of this informational regime is concentrated in the supplier, the distribution of the burden cannot remain blind to this asymmetry. Otherwise, the duty to inform becomes a comforting fiction for the platform and an evidentiary nightmare for the consumer. The content of transparency needs to be institutionally reconstructible, or its protection dissolves into formalism.

The objective is to prevent the platform from converting documentary excess into a safe-conduct, dismantling the rhetoric that all available information equals adequate information and putting the duty to inform back on its proper axis, which is that of practical utility for consent, comparison and control. In IOCs, this means shifting the analysis from “the text exists” to “the essential meaning was really placed in conditions to be understood”. The CDC, read functionally, does not protect the supplier who documents too much. It protects the consumer who needs to decide on the basis of what really matters. It is this reading that allows one to move, in the following stages, from the critique of noise to the demand for open auditability and to the reconstruction of enjoyment as a position that cannot be degraded under cover of pseudo-transparency.

The duty to inform, in the CDC system, is not fulfilled by the mere multiplication of texts, links, cross-references, windows, policies and documents formally available to the consumer. Informing, in a material key, means making cognizable in a clear, adequate and conspicuous way the essential content of the consumer relationship, especially that which defines the utility of the performance, its conditions of enjoyment and its relevant risks. This is exactly what is highlighted when interpreting Article 31 of the CDC, affirming that the supplier must ensure the consumer “clear, precise and conspicuous information about the main characteristics of the product”, including data related to its characteristics, its economic repercussion, health and safety <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 877)</2>. As a reflection of the principle of transparency, the supplier must offer “clear and correct” information about the qualities of the product and the conditions of the contract, drafting the text clearly, so as to “give the consumer the opportunity” to know the content of the obligations assumed, on pain of the contract not binding them, “even if duly formalized” <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 820-821)</4>. Practices of merely performative transparency, therefore, can constitute a violation of the duty to inform. <5>↩</5>

The duty to inform, in the CDC, is not satisfied by a merely quantitative logic. It is not enough for the supplier to dump documents, links, clauses or blocks of text on the consumer and then claim formal transparency. The legal duty requires positive action aimed at the information actually reaching its recipient in conditions that allow relevant understanding. For this reason, “in the regime of consumer relations, the duty to inform the consumer requires an active posture from the supplier”, it being the supplier who “must make the information reach the consumer” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 207)</2>. The mere formal provision of content, therefore, is not enough, because there can be documentary access without true cognitive appropriation. The consumer's right to information constitutes “a much more complex question than just a problem of lack of information that needs to be ensured” <3>Wada</3><4>(Beales, Craswell e Salop apud Wada, 2016, p. 82)</4>. The duty to inform, thus, is fulfilled not by volume, by documentary accumulation or by mere formal opening of access, but by informational adequacy. <5>↩</5>

Excess, dispersion, complexity and low hierarchization of the essential characterize forms of functional opacity produced under the appearance of transparency. The starting point lies in the refusal of the simplistic premise according to which it would suffice to add more information to resolve the consumer's informational vulnerability. By recording that the right to information is “a much more complex question than just a problem of lack of information that needs to be ensured” <1>Wada</1><2>(Beales, Craswell e Salop apud Wada, 2016, p. 82)</2>, the logic of mere documentary filling is set aside. This obscurity appears when information is formally provided, but organized in a way that makes comparison and identification of what really matters unfeasible. This is what occurs, for example, in banking packages with numerous products that do not correspond to one another, making it “very difficult for the consumer to compare the benefit packages offered by banks” <3>Wada</3><4>(Wada, 2016, p. 168-169)</4>. The abusive practice may occur when there is material interference with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms and conditions of the product or service, with an excessive advantage obtained from the lack of understanding of the risks, costs or conditions involved <5>Wada</5><6>(Wada, 2016, p. 141-142)</6>. In this key, performative transparency is defined precisely by the conspicuous display of content whose form of presentation produces functional opacity. <7>↩</7>

“Paragraph 3. Written adhesion contracts shall be drafted in clear terms and with conspicuous and legible characters, so as to facilitate their understanding by the consumer. Paragraph 4. Clauses that imply a limitation of the consumer's rights shall be drafted with emphasis, allowing their immediate and easy understanding.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.. <3>↩</3>

Adequate information, in the consumer-law regime, is not defined by the simple existence of available content, but by its aptitude to present the essential elements of the contracting at the exact moment the consumer needs to decide. For this reason, “information about the performance of the obligation is essential for the consumer” and, “without it, it is not possible to make conscious choices about the product acquired or even about the service contracted” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 206)</2>. This requirement gains density in the prior estimate as a qualified moment of decision, in which the consumer can examine “the quality of the service, the deadline for execution, the materials used”, in short, the essential elements that make up the price and the substance of the performance, being also able to clarify doubts and negotiate the terms before binding themselves <3>Wada</3><4>(Wada, 2016, p. 211)</4>. Informational adequacy requires organized presentation of the essential content in useful time for deliberation. When the structure of the offer “reduces price transparency”, “the comparability of offers” is hindered <5>Wada</5><6>(Wada, 2016, p. 168)</6>, which directly compromises the practical freedom of choice. Adequate information, thus, is that which allows one to use and compare the essential before the decision, and not that which merely exists in some remote corner of the contractual ecosystem. <7>↩</7>

The legal sufficiency of information, in the CDC, is not to be confused with its mere formal availability or with the existence of a body of documents the consumer could potentially consult. Excessive cross-references, opaque chains, overly long texts or a documentary architecture that hinders apprehension of the real content of the obligation do not satisfy the duty to inform in the material sense. No average consumer could understand obligations assumed in contracts that pile up cross-references to laws and provisional measures in an incomprehensible way, which is why such a bond can be undone for failure of transparency (in this case good faith) at the time of its formation, since the consumer could not understand what obligations they were assuming <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 903)</2>. For general conditions to be included, “the simple mention” that they will be used “is not enough”; the consumer must “be able to read and understand” what the clauses mean, and such texts frequently appear in a “somewhat furtive” way, in long or hard-to-read material <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 91-92)</4>. Consequently, documentary excess and formal availability have legal value only if they preserve the material intelligibility of the essential content of the relationship. <5>↩</5>

Advertising, in IOC ecosystems, cannot be treated as a peripheral layer of the offer. It participates directly in the production of the economic meaning of the object, organizes the <1>p. 624</1> consumer's expectation before enjoyment and anticipates, to a large extent, the way in which utility, value, rarity, performance and equivalence will be perceived. It is precisely for this reason that consumer-law protection needs to treat it as a controllable semiotic mechanism. The problem lies not only in literally false sentences or in gross omissions. It lies in the strategic management of the visible and the invisible, of what gains emphasis and what is relegated to the documentary background, of what appears as an immediate advantage and what recedes as a cost, limitation or ordinary risk of the supply.

In platform markets, this question gains special density because the promised experience is not static. The advertised object will later be subjected to updating, curation, parameterization, <1>enforcement</1> and ordinary reconfigurations of the environment. This means that the expectation is not only formed before contracting; it can also be strategically overproduced before the consumer has any real chance to perceive mutability, limits of use, equivalence criteria and ordinary possibilities of functional downgrading. In IOCs, advertising does not announce only an object. It announces a future governed experience. And, for that very reason, it can produce error not only through express falsity, but through the semiotic construction of a trust incompatible with the reality of the regime of enjoyment.

The first point is, then, to recognize advertising as market semiotics. It does not operate only by transferring objective data, but through signs, framings, visual hierarchies and inductions of reading. The relevant vulnerability here is not a lack of technical information in the narrow sense, nor a diffuse psychic weakness of the consumer. What matters is the asymmetry of meaning produced by communication designed to guide adhesion under conditions of selective visibility. The marketing message defines what appears as an advantage, what is naturalized as tolerable, what is anticipated as rarity and what is concealed as an ordinary consequence of the contracting. We are not facing promotional ornament. We are facing a structure for the production of expectation.

This conclusion is perfectly compatible with the dogmatics of the CDC. When advertising contains sufficiently precise elements about qualities, conditions, advantages or characteristics of the object, it becomes part of the offer and radiates obligational effects over the consumer relationship<1><2>713</2></1>. The consumer-law system breaks, therefore, with the old privatist view according to <3>p. 625</3> which advertising would be a simple invitation indifferent to the contracting. In more direct language: the promotional message enters the contract through the door of trust. If the supplier organizes the market through promises, signals and sufficiently guiding descriptions, it cannot later pretend that all of that was only aesthetic ambiance and that the real bond was hidden, dry and hostile, in later clauses. Advertising participates in the very shaping of the legally enforceable performance.

Here, therefore, objective good faith does not appear as an agreeable abstraction, but as a concrete matrix of ancillary duties in marketing communication. Fair advertising is not merely advertising “without lies”. It is advertising structured in a way compatible with legitimate trust, identification of its persuasive character and consistency between what produces expectation and what will actually be delivered. Good faith requires that the supplier promise only what it can fulfill and, if it provides information about characteristics of the product, the service or the conditions of contracting, that this information be correct, truthful and apt to guide the formation of will<1><2>714</2></1>. This matters a great deal in IOCs because expectation is usually formed before the consumer has any real contact with the ordinary regime of mutability of the object. The promise circulates first. The frustration comes later.

From this follows the third point: advertising deceptiveness does not depend on a literal lie. The CDC does not require frontal, caricatural or gross falsity to recognize deception. Unlawfulness can arise when the message, even if it contains literally true elements, is apt to lead the consumer into error through ambiguity, relevant omission, strategic incompleteness or <1>p. 626</1> simple persuasive organization of the visible<2><3>715</3></2>. The error need not be fabricated by the openly false sentence. It can be produced by the way the essential is hierarchized, by selective emphasis on advantages and by the displacement of relevant conditions to <4>disclaimers</4>, layers of low visibility, later links or discursive zones that do not usefully integrate the moment of decision.

This is the core of misleading advertising by semiotic architecture. The architecture of an advertisement becomes legally relevant when the supplier structures the consumer's understanding so as to reinforce the positive side of the experience and push the onerous, mutable or limited side out of focus. Put more simply, communication need not lie in order to deceive. It is enough that it manages the interpretive framing in a sufficiently asymmetrical way. Advertising can tell the truth in pieces and still lie as a whole. It can keep the real cost out of the visual center. It can suggest a functional equivalence that the ordinary regime of the IOC later downgrades without verifiable correspondence. It can speak of rarity, urgency, exclusivity or status without adequately integrating, on the same plane of emphasis, the precariousness, reversibility or mutability of what is being acquired.

This mode of operation intensifies when the platform organizes pre-deliveries of expectation. <1>Teasers</1>, storefronts, <2>trailers</2>, event campaigns, passes, rarity panels, countdown timers, suggested equivalences, narratives of distinction and communication through influencers are not merely advance publicity. They are mechanisms for curating expectation before actual enjoyment. In IOCs, this matters enormously because the governance of the decision begins before the purchase and before acceptance. The platform builds in advance what the consumer expects to find, to value, to fear losing and to tolerate as admissible frustration. The marketing environment thus already functions as an architecture of future tolerable disappointment. If expectation is inflated by a semiotics of value and later absorbed <3>p. 627</3> by an ordinary regime of downgrading, elastic equivalence or unilateral mutability, advertising was not merely a pre-contractual stage. It was a mechanism for capturing trust.

In this context, the case of hybrid formats is especially important. In digital ecosystems, advertising, content, entertainment, recommendation and sale frequently blur into one another. Influencers, creators, “community” posts, demonstrations, in-game storefronts and events mediated by the platform's own environment blur the distinction between descriptive communication, cultural recommendation and marketing persuasion. This hybridization weakens the intelligibility of the message's advertising character and compromises communicational fairness. The consumer need not be facing a banner explicitly labeled as an advertisement to be persuasively steered toward a purchase. When the marketing character becomes harder to identify, the semiotic asymmetry deepens, because advertising is no longer perceived as advertising and comes to operate disguised as experience, recommendation or mere ecosystem content.

It is precisely for this reason that Article 38 of the CDC proves so important here. The burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of advertising information or communication lies with whoever sponsors it<1><2>716</2></1>. This is no elegant evidentiary detail. It is a normative recognition that advertising is a space of power and, therefore, of responsibility. In IOCs, this provision spares the consumer from having to prove alone that the expectation produced by the communication was incompatible with the actual regime of enjoyment. If the platform advertises a certain equivalence, benefit, utility, standard of stability or implicit value of rarity, it is for the platform to demonstrate with documents that this narrative is correct in light of what is ordinarily delivered and administered in the ecosystem. The system does not presume the innocence of the marketing promise. It requires that whoever produced it back it up.

This logic is closely bound up with the protection of trust. Legally protected trust arises not only from the final contractual instrument, but also from the supplier's communicational conduct in the market<1><2>717</2></1>. The more precise, eloquent <3>p. 628</3> and directive the advertising, the greater its capacity to generate legitimate expectation and, therefore, the greater its binding force. This is decisive because it blocks the old maneuver of capturing trust in the pre-contractual phase and then trying to drain it away in the final text of the contract or in mutable internal rules. Advertising does not stay outside, since it takes part in the legally relevant core of the consumer relationship. If it organizes expectation, it also organizes the yardstick by which frustration will be measured.

The rules on advertising to children function here as a normative limit case that reinforces this reading from within, without shifting the axis of the discussion. The point is not to equate adults with children, nor to open a new thematic front. The point is to show that the CDC itself already recognizes that abusiveness may arise from taking advantage of a structural deficiency of judgment exploited by persuasive communication. When the system deems abusive the advertising that takes advantage of a child's deficiency of judgment and experience, it explicitly recognizes that the manipulation of meaning and the exploitation of limits on decoding are legally relevant. The most important normative datum is not childhood itself, but the underlying logic. When communication takes advantage of a structural asymmetry of understanding, the control of abusiveness intensifies. This reinforces, from within the system itself, the legitimacy of treating semiotic vulnerability as a legal fact and not as a sociological metaphor.

The argumentative value of this limit case is quite elegant. It shows that the CDC already operates with gradations of vulnerability tied to real conditions of understanding and resistance, and not only to an occasional lack of data. Advertising can be abusive even without lying, simply because it exploits a structural limitation of judgment. Transposing this reasoning to IOCs in a controlled way, without infantilizing the adult consumer, one may argue that there are also situations in which architecture, curation and private governance of meaning produce real asymmetries of decoding, comparison and proof. When advertising and the platform's communicational environment systematically exploit these asymmetries, room opens for heightened control of deceptiveness and abusiveness.

The immediate dogmatic consequence is that advertising in IOCs must be treated as a controllable practice when the essential is kept out of focus and the negative is pushed into <1>p. 629</1> <2>disclaimers</2> or useless cross-references; when marketing communication, through anticipatory curation of expectation, produces an image of value, rarity, performance or functional equivalence that the ordinary regime of mutability later frustrates without verifiable correspondence; and when the marketing character of the message is weakened by hybrid formats that conflate content, recommendation, entertainment and sale. In these cases, deceptiveness is not reduced to a literal lie. It appears as a defect in the very architecture of the promise.

It is therefore necessary to connect semiotic vulnerability, good faith, trust, deceptiveness and abusiveness without psychologizing consumption or resorting to moralism against advertising as such. The problem is not desiring, fantasizing or attributing symbolic value to the object. The problem arises when the marketing production of expectation is organized so as to steer the consumer's understanding toward an image of the object that the supply regime itself does not sustain, or sustains only under hidden reservations, opaque equivalences and silent mutability. Advertising thus ceases to be merely an announcement and becomes an objective element in the production of a legally controllable trust.

This prepares the transition to the broader decision environment in which advertising, information, interface and choice architecture operate in an integrated way. Advertising will not be the only gear of semiotic vulnerability, but it is one of its most powerful cores. It pre-shapes expectation, organizes the imaginary of value, distributes visibility and conditions what the consumer understands as risk, opportunity and loss. In IOCs, where enjoyment is governed and mutable, this makes it one of the CDC's main points of control. The supplier answers not only for what it promises in isolated sentences. It answers for the regime of meaning it produces when it advertises.

Under the Consumer Protection Code, advertising does not occupy a merely peripheral or ornamental position. When the advertising message contains sufficiently precise elements about the object, its qualities, conditions or advantages, it becomes part of the offer and radiates obligational effects over the consumer relationship, binding the supplier to the content conveyed <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 140-142)</2>. The consequence is direct: advertising does not remain outside the contract as a mere prior persuasive stage, but takes part in shaping the legally enforceable content of the performance. This logic is reinforced by the abandonment of the old private-law understanding that treated advertising as a harmless invitation to contract. In the consumer-law system, the marketing message is no longer legally indifferent and comes to function as a source of obligation whenever, by its degree of precision and capacity to form expectation, it makes up the content of the offer addressed to the consumer <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 144)</4>. If advertising is part of the offer and creates binding obligations, then the way it organizes the consumer's understanding, ranks elements, distributes visibility and produces expectation also becomes legally relevant. The advertising message does not stand outside the relationship doing marketing; it takes part in the very obligational structure of the supply. <5>↩</5>

Under the CDC regime, marketing communication is subject to substantive control of fairness, truthfulness and adequacy because it can shape the consumer's legitimate expectation even before the bond is formalized. Marques states that, in matters of advertising, objective good faith requires it to be “a fair activity”, also considered from the standpoint of whoever receives the message, so that it promises only what it can deliver and, if it provides information about characteristics of the product, the service or the contractual conditions, that information is correct and truthful <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 832; p. 886)</2>. The author adds that the main characteristic of misleading advertising, under the CDC, is that it is liable to lead the consumer into error, including by “omissions”, and that the rule must be interpreted broadly, since the error consists in a “false notion of reality” potentially formed in the consumer's mind by the advertising <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 909)</4>. Applied to the problem of semiotic architecture, this guideline authorizes control of promotional messages that, without lying outright, organize the interpretive field of the offer so as to produce an illusory understanding of utility, extent, stability or conditions of enjoyment. <5>↩</5>

Advertising deceptiveness, under the CDC, does not depend on literal falsity or on an outright, demonstrable lie. Unlawfulness may arise whenever the message, even if partly true, is capable of leading the consumer into error, including through omission, ambiguity, relevant incompleteness or the very form in which the content is presented <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 167)</2>. The decisive point is not the microscopic truthfulness of each isolated sentence, but the deceptive potential of the communication as a meaningful whole, as actually perceived by its recipient. This perception becomes especially important when the essential datum is pushed into zones of low visibility, diluted in accessory information or weakened by graphic and drafting strategies that reduce how well it is grasped in practice. Deceptiveness may emerge, for example, when the real price does not appear clearly, when charges are relegated to a visually insignificant position or when the decisive information is technically included but functionally hidden in the context of the piece <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 168)</4>. Misleading advertising by semiotic architecture does not require gross falsity. It can operate through the strategic management of the visible and the invisible, through the functional ambiguity of language and through the persuasive organization of the advertisement, so as to steer the consumer's understanding away from what really matters. <5>↩</5>
“Art. 38. The burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of the advertising information or communication lies with whoever sponsors it.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>.. <3>↩</3>

In consumer law, advertising takes a direct part in the formation of contractual trust. This is because, in markets marked by lean, opaque or incomplete adhesion contracts, the marketing message often anticipates, completes and thickens the understanding the consumer forms of the utility, qualities and mode of enjoyment of the object offered, and becomes a relevant element in building their legitimate expectation <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 142)</2>. Legally protected trust therefore arises not only from the final contractual instrument, but also from the supplier's communicational conduct in the market. This binding effect can be understood in light of the protection of the expectation created by the advertiser's own conduct. The more eloquent, precise and directive the message, the greater its capacity to generate trust worthy of protection and, therefore, the greater its binding force <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, p. 42)</4>. Advertising does not merely describe the object; it pre-shapes the expectation of enjoyment that will later serve as the yardstick for assessing performance, inadequacy and deceptiveness. When marketing communication structures the consumer's expectation, it enters the legally relevant core of the consumer relationship and may be a source both of obligation and of legally censurable frustration. <5>↩</5>

<1>6.2.4 </1>On semiotic vulnerability as a contemporary form of factual vulnerability

To be of dogmatic use, semiotic vulnerability cannot be treated as a loose cultural metaphor or as a judgment about the consumer's psychology. It designates a <1>p. 580</1> contemporary form of factual vulnerability produced by the way supply is organized in platform environments. In IOCs, the relevant asymmetry does not lie only in the fact that the consumer knows less about the system's internal characteristics. It arises because the platform controls the very instruments that make the relationship intelligible, that is, the signs, interfaces, metrics, framings and records through which the consumer forms expectations, assesses enjoyment, perceives downgrading and tries to mount a challenge. The consumer's vulnerability remains the pillar of the CDC's special protection, and it is precisely for this reason that semiotic vulnerability must be understood as a contemporary specification of this structural datum, and not as a parallel or extravagant category <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 324; p. 307)</3><4><5>650</5></4>.

This point calls for an important distinction. Semiotic vulnerability does not describe the user's lesser individual discernment, psychological naivety or subjective susceptibility. The problem lies in the objective way the environment organizes language, visibility, comparison and proof. On platforms, the consumer depends on governed mediations to understand what they acquired, to perceive whether the experience was altered and to identify whether a legally relevant loss occurred. This means that the platform not only supplies the object, but also administers the reference points through which that object can be perceived and measured. The asymmetry, then, is no longer merely informational in the classical sense and becomes semiotic as well, because the supplier controls the regime through which the meaning of enjoyment itself is produced.

It is precisely this that sustains the category under the CDC. The consumer's vulnerability does not act merely as the system's sociological backdrop. It is normatively linked to good faith, the duty to inform, transparency and the protection of trust. The consumer's autonomy depends on positive duties to inform, to cooperate and to act with fairness and care, because without this minimum standard of conduct the decision to contract is not rational in a <1>p. 581</1> legally relevant sense <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 812; p. 1480)</3><4><5>651</5></4>. Semiotic vulnerability is anchored precisely in this mechanism. It shows that, in governed environments, the duty to inform cannot be reduced to a bureaucratic dumping of data or to rituals of acceptance. What is at stake is the creation of minimum conditions for actually understanding enjoyment and its relevant alterations.

For this reason, informational inadequacy is not limited to simple omission. The supplier may appear transparent and still produce material opacity through excess, dispersion, low practical utility, overly technical language or a communicational organization that frustrates understanding. Ensuring formal access to information is not enough. It must be correct, clear, precise and conspicuous, without useless prolixity or strategic scarcity, and the supplier may not set up barriers that negatively interfere with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms and conditions of the contract <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 207; p. 142)</2><3><4>652</4></3>. Once again, this makes it possible to formulate semiotic vulnerability without psychologizing the consumer. The problem is not inner weakness. The problem is a communicational architecture that appears to inform while organizing noise.

A decisive consequence follows: in IOCs, the platform controls not only the modulation of the object. It also controls the means by which that modulation can be perceived, named and compared. Storefronts, metrics, rarities, narratives of prestige, <1>p. 582</1> reputational systems, visual <2>feedbacks</2>, progression histories and interface framings are no longer peripheral elements of the environment and become part of the intelligibility of the consumed object itself. When these elements are reorganized unilaterally, the relevant loss may be obscured under an appearance of continuity. The consumer keeps nominal access, but loses functional or symbolic utility without finding clear criteria to measure the erosion. It is this kind of asymmetry that the category seeks to make visible.

The CDC already offers instruments for this, because the problem is not confined to the abstract plane of communication. Abusive practices involve precisely the supplier's use of its position of power to impose conduct on the consumer in violation of the duties of fairness, cooperation and respect for legitimate expectations. Abusiveness may also arise from the asymmetrical exploitation of the relevant meanings of the consumer relationship, especially when lengthy, obscure or surprising clauses compromise the quality of the information and the adhering party's consent <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 328-329; p. 388)</2><3><4>653</4></3>. Semiotic vulnerability thus remains within the trunk of consumer law. It merely names more precisely a current form of exploiting a vulnerability that the system's institutes already intuited.

This reading also clarifies why the “governed environment” does not compete with the “immaterial product”. In the IOC regime, the governed environment is a condition for the legal existence of the consumed product itself. The object can be enjoyed only while the platform maintains, administers and modulates access, signs, rules of use and parameters of intelligibility. This means that the environment is not an external frame of the performance, but a constitutive element of the product as legally consumed. Relevant alterations in the architecture of enjoyment may correspond, in dogmatic terms, to alterations of the object of consumption itself. <1>p. 583</1> Semiotic vulnerability makes intelligible precisely the asymmetry this arrangement generates, because the platform administers both the object and the means of reading it.

This category also reorganizes classic problems of the CDC. If enjoyment depends on continuous maintenance and modulation, delivery cannot be conceived as a purely one-off act. If utility can be reconfigured, inadequacy is not limited to the obvious defect of a static thing. If there is no clear endpoint of performance, identifying the quality defect must take into account the real moment when the degradation becomes perceptible and verifiable. If the promise circulates through signs, advertising, narratives and interfaces, the correspondence between offer and enjoyment cannot be measured solely by the letter of a contractual text. Semiotic vulnerability thus functions as a category for attributing the structural asymmetry that justifies reconstructing the duty to inform, trust, adequacy and abusiveness in an opaque and mutable environment.

This problem bears directly on proof. In technically sophisticated ecosystems, the supplier controls not only the service, but also the documents, the records, the technique and the very intelligibility of the relationship. Often the consumer's difficulty is not only economic, but factual and technical. The necessary evidence is not in their hands. It lies with whoever administers the environment, the <1>logs</1>, the parameter settings and the relevant histories.

Facilitating the consumer's defense and redistributing the burden of proof become decisive in relationships of this kind. The technological specialization of the service and the supplier's dominant position make the reversal of the burden of proof, in many cases, the only instrument capable of actually enabling consumer protection <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 854; p. 283)</2><3><4>654</4></3>. Semiotic vulnerability is, at this point, also evidentiary vulnerability.

Consumer protection, then, is not satisfied by formally available information. It requires contracting that is informed and conscious to a degree sufficient for the consumer to know, decide on and properly use the product or service. The information <1>p. 584</1> the system protects is valued for its practical usefulness in offsetting vulnerability, and not as a bureaucratic ritual of offloading data <2>Wada</2><3>(Wada, 2016, p. 211; p. 143)</3><4><5>655</5></4>. On platforms, this means that intelligibility is not communicational ornament. It is a functional prerequisite for the decision-making usefulness of information itself and, therefore, for the legitimacy of the supply.

The foundational basis of the category's dogmatic usefulness is thus identified. Semiotic vulnerability neither replaces the <1>standards</1> formulated nor merges with them. It identifies the relevant structural asymmetry in IOCs and allows the problem to be brought back to classic CDC categories without reducing the dispute to a “mere environmental problem” external to the object. On that basis, the next steps of the argument become manageable, in particular the requirement of institutional verifiability, the reconstruction of adequacy in terms of functional integrity and a more realistic allocation of the burden of proof in the face of opaque and governed mutations of enjoyment.

To remain dogmatically useful, the formulation of semiotic vulnerability must be understood as a contemporary development of a structural datum that already organizes the consumer-law microsystem: the consumer's vulnerability as the permanent foundation of the CDC's protective interpretation. The point is not to create a parallel category, cut off from the system's grammar, but to specify, in the context of platforms, one of the ways in which the imbalance of power between supplier and consumer manifests itself today. Marques puts this quite directly when she states that, in consumer contracts, "the problem is the flagrant imbalance of power between the contracting parties. One of the parties is vulnerable (art. 4º. I), it is the weaker pole of the contractual relationship, since it cannot discuss the content of the contract", and as a rule can only accept or reject the pre-drafted package <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 324)</2>. The author adds that the definition of consumer is "the pillar that sustains the special protection", because that protection exists only by reason of the consumer party's vulnerability in market relations <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 307)</4>. Seen this way, semiotic vulnerability appears as a contemporary form of factual vulnerability, traceable to good faith, the duty to inform, the protection of trust and contractual balance. <5>↩</5>

Under the CDC, the consumer's vulnerability does not act merely as a sociological premise of the protective regime; it is normatively linked to objective good faith and the duty to inform, forming an operative core for containing the market's typical asymmetries. This means that the consumer's structural fragility is addressed in law by imposing positive duties on the supplier, above all in the formation and conduct of the contractual relationship. Marques makes this mechanism explicit when she stresses that the idea of "rational autonomy" depends precisely on ancillary duties to inform, to cooperate and to treat the consumer with fairness and care, since only with this "new standard of conduct in the market" can the consumer reach a "truly reflected, autonomous and 'rational" will <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 812)</2>. Along the same lines, the author states that the CDC seeks "transparency and harmony in consumer relations", imposing good faith as a requirement to prevent market practices from "making use of consumers' vulnerability", with the duty to inform being "a basic duty of suppliers" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1480)</4>. This keeps semiotic vulnerability anchored in the normative ground of the microsystem. <5>↩</5>

In this sense, Wada (20216) helps show that informational inadequacy, in consumer law, is not reduced to the simple absence of data. The failure may also arise when the supplier ensures only formal access to information, but does so under conditions that frustrate its practical intelligibility. The problem, then, is not only omission, but communication that is materially insufficient, through excess, dispersion, complexity or little concrete usefulness. Along these lines, the author expressly states that “it is not enough to ensure formal access to information”, and that it must have the legally required attributes of “correctness, clarity, precision and conspicuousness” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 207)</2>. The requirement is qualitative, not merely quantitative. Seen this way, informational noise also makes the consumer vulnerable. Information must be “precise (= neither prolix nor scarce)”, precisely so that it remains comprehensible and serviceable to the consumer's decision-making <3>Wada</3><4>(Marques apud Wada, 2016, p. 207)</4>. The author further observes that the supplier may not interfere “significantly and negatively with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms or conditions” of the contract, nor set up “barriers or difficulties” to understanding <5>Wada</5><6>(Wada, 2016, p. 142)</6>. Hence the relevance of treating semiotic vulnerability as a contemporary form of factual vulnerability: not because the consumer is psychologically weak, but because they may be exposed to communicational architectures that appear transparent while producing material opacity. <7>↩</7>

The formulation of semiotic vulnerability remains internal to the CDC when it is read through the interplay of vulnerability, good faith, the duty to inform, trust and abusive practices. Abusive practices involve a breach of the supplier's duty of fairness toward the consumer, notably, in many cases, through the supplier's use of its position and power to impose a certain conduct on the consumer. In these cases, there is a breach of the duties of fairness, cooperation and respect for legitimate expectations arising from objective good faith, which include positive duties of clarification and transparent advice, as well as a duty to refrain from conduct that takes advantage of vulnerability and affects the consumer's freedom to negotiate <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 328-329)</2>. This reading is reinforced in the treatment of surprise clauses. Their abusiveness stems, even before any breach of balance in the strict sense, from the breach of the duty to inform the consumer, above all in overly long or complex contracts entered into by a lay consumer. In these situations, the supplier bears a duty of adequate clarification, failing which informational insufficiency is presumed and the quality of consent is compromised <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 388)</4>. The category of semiotic vulnerability thus does not abandon the trunk of consumer law; it merely names more precisely a contemporary form of factual vulnerability that its own institutes already intuited: the asymmetrical exploitation of the relevant meanings of the consumer relationship. <5>↩</5>

The CDC's response to contemporary asymmetries is not limited to the substantive plane of information and abusiveness; it already extends to the procedural plane of proof. The specialization and technological sophistication of products and services, combined with the consumer's economic or technical weakness, make the reversal of the burden of proof, in many cases, the only means capable of allowing the claim to succeed. This is explained by the supplier's dominant position, since it holds in-depth technical knowledge and controls documents, records and the contracting process itself <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 854)</2>. Often the consumer cannot prove their case simply because the necessary evidence is not in their hands but in the supplier's. This is not merely an economic obstacle, but a factual impossibility tied to the lack of conditions, including technical ones, for producing evidence, because the power of direction and specialized knowledge belong, as a rule, to the supplier <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 283)</4>. Seen this way, semiotic vulnerability can also be perceived as a contemporary form of evidentiary vulnerability: whoever controls not only the service, but the records, the technique and the intelligibility of the relationship, also controls much of the conditions for challenging it. The CDC already responds to this by redistributing burdens and facilitating the defense. <5>↩</5>

Consumer protection is directly tied to the requirement of information that is not merely formally available, but materially capable of guiding a decision. Legally adequate communication must produce genuinely informed and conscious contracting, that is, a state of understanding sufficient for the consumer to know what they are binding themselves to and to deliberate with a minimum of autonomy. For this reason, Wada states that, for the normative program of protection against abusive commercial practices, it is essential to ensure the consumer “informed and conscious contracting”, since “only thus will they be able to make their decision and enter into the commitment with the supplier” <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 211)</2>. This requirement has a clearly rebalancing function. The information the consumer-law system protects has no value in itself, as a bureaucratic rite of offloading data, but for its practical usefulness in offsetting the consumer's vulnerability. The author observes that this limit on the supplier seeks precisely to “rebalance the consumer relationship”, giving the consumer the opportunity to “know, negotiate and decide” <3>Wada</3><4>(Wada, 2016, p. 211)</4>. Along the same lines, the author maintains that, given the consumer's lack of capacity to choose or use the product or service properly, the supplier comes under a duty to provide the performance under conditions that allow the consumer to “make their choices and use the product or service properly” <5>Wada</5><6>(Wada, 2016, p. 143)</6>. Intelligibility, therefore, is not communicational adornment: it is a functional prerequisite for the decision-making usefulness of information. <7>↩</7>

In platform contexts, information, advertising and abusive practices cannot be examined as autonomous phenomena, isolated in watertight compartments, because, in the real process of consumption, they work together to form expectation, urgency, trust and tolerance of frustration. The legal problem is no longer exhausted by asking whether a given clause existed, whether certain information was technically available or whether an advertisement contained a literal falsehood. What needs to be controlled is the integrated decision-making arrangement through which the platform organizes the consumer's joining of and staying in the <1>p. 630</1> ecosystem, distributing visibility, scarcity, comparability and the promise of value in ways that serve its own interests. In IOCs, this becomes even more delicate because the consumed object does not settle into a thing delivered once and for all. The consumer's decision concerns a future governed experience, continuously modulated by architecture, curation and <2>enforcement</2>, so that the initial expectation becomes part of the very legal substance of enjoyment.

This finding calls for an important methodological shift. Information cannot be read only as declaratory content; advertising cannot be treated as promotional ornament; and abusive practice cannot be reduced to a marginal event after the contract. What exists, in many cases, is a single communicational and decision-making environment in which promise, selective visibility, managed scarcity, symbolic rewards, choice architecture and rituals of acceptance act together to produce adhesion. Within this frame, transparency is not a mere formal requirement of the final moment of contracting, but a prerequisite that must run through the consumer's entire approach to the object, from the capture of their attention to the settling of their expectation about what will be obtained, lost or tolerated as admissible frustration<1><2>718</2></1>. For this reason, the legality of the relationship cannot be assessed solely by the final text of the bond, but by the whole set of pre-contractual and contextual manifestations that shaped the consumer's will and perception of risk.

It is precisely within this framework that hypercuratorial anticipation acquires dogmatic relevance. The platform does not administer only the present experience of enjoyment. Before that, it administers the very horizon of expectation on which the consumer bases the decision. Temporary events, selected storefronts, curated rarity, artificial urgency, promises of distinction, the teasing of utility, suggested equivalences and cycles of emotional intensification make up a grammar of anticipation that acts on how the consumer learns to desire, to expect and to fear loss. The environment comes to govern not only access to the object, but the future interpretation of its value. This <1>p. 631</1> profoundly alters how information, advertising and abusiveness are read, because the promise is no longer a side phenomenon. It becomes a structural component of the regime of governed enjoyment.

In these contexts, the platform produces something more sophisticated than ordinary commercial persuasion. It builds cycles of promise, intensification and partial delivery, in which the object is presented as a rare, prestigious, limited or virtually guaranteed opportunity, even though actual enjoyment depends on later mechanisms of randomness, mutability, internal rebalancing or unilaterally defined equivalences. The consumer is induced to join not only by a stated advantage, but by an architecture of expectation that teaches them to read that acquisition as a decisive moment, an imminent loss or a unique chance. The decision is thus formed within an environment that administers the meaning of value in advance. And it is precisely there that relevant omission, misleading advertising and abusiveness may arise together, with no need for an outright lie or a complete absence of information.

Relevant omission appears when the essential is deliberately pushed out of the decision-making focus. The supplier emphasizes urgency, benefit, rarity or prestige, but relegates to side conditions what really defines the substance of enjoyment, such as relevant limits on use, the object's ordinary mutability, equivalence parameters, possible losses, narrow windows of use, additional requirements for the promise to materialize or specific conditions for keeping the advertised value. Misleading advertising, in turn, manifests itself when the image of utility or equivalence built by the promotional environment finds no verifiable correspondence in the actual experience of enjoyment, either because the platform later downgrades the object, or because the initial promise already concealed, through ambiguity or an architecture of visibility, the real way in which utility would be delivered. Abusive advertising, finally, appears when the design of the environment systematically exploits the consumer's vulnerability, compressing their room for deliberation through artificial urgency, symbolic reward, the ritualization of acceptance and the fragmentation of the relevant conditions.

This reading avoids two symmetrical errors. The first would be to moralize every technique of commercial persuasion, as if all intense advertising, all interface curation or all architecture aimed at conversion were unlawful in itself. That is not the case. The market may promote, persuade, dramatize and organize interest. What the CDC does not allow is for this organization of interest to operate through functional opacity, the capture of expectation and the displacement of the essential out of the useful field of understanding. The second error would be to imagine that a problem exists only when an advertisement, taken in isolation, contains a literal falsehood or when a given <1>p. 632</1> clause, taken in isolation, is abusive. In contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, unlawfulness may lie precisely in the combination of elements that seem neutral when seen separately but that, combined, govern the consumer's decision in a structurally asymmetrical way.

At this point, advertising needs to be returned to its correct dogmatic place. It is neither external to the contract nor mere cultural ambiance of the market. Marketing communication takes an active part in manufacturing the disposition to contract, stoking needs, organizing desires and at the same time presenting the path to their satisfaction<1><2>719</2></1>. Instead of a clean, compartmentalized sequence of advertisement, information and contracting, what exists is a communicational continuum in which the platform produces expectation, guides the reading of the object, manages the pace of the decision and only then stabilizes acceptance in documentary forms that often fail to reflect, with the same emphasis, the promise that triggered the bond. This means that abusiveness cannot be located only in the final statement, because the pre-contractual environment itself already takes part in the material constitution of consent.

This conclusion is reinforced by the observation that, on platforms, marketing communication often dissolves into hybrid formats. Recommendation, entertainment, tutorial, community narrative, product demonstration, influencer content and advertisement blur together, lowering the consumer's critical vigilance and muddling the perception of the message's persuasive status. In these cases, the legal problem lies not only in the content communicated but in the very way it is inserted into the decision flow, making it less intelligible that this is a commercial push and maximizing its capacity to produce adhesion<1><2>720</2></1>. The abusive arrangement, then, does not depend on an <3>p. 633</3> explicit banner or a classic advertisement. It may reside precisely in this dissolution of advertising into the environment, which makes it more effective as a technique for steering behavior and more opaque as a source of obligation and control.

This has direct consequences for the relationship between information, advertising and abusive practices. In IOCs, the supplier does not merely transmit messages about a pre-given object. It manages signs and metrics that constitute the very perceived value of enjoyment. Advertising does not surround the object from outside; it helps produce it as an expectation of performance, distinction, utility or permanence. Information does not serve only to describe this object; it determines how far the consumer can understand its real conditions of use and its ordinary margins of alteration. And an abusive practice does not appear only when there is brutal imposition or an outrageous clause; it can emerge from a decision ecosystem in which urgency, scarcity, performative transparency and elastic equivalences work together to induce adhesion in a context of materially defective understanding.

In this context, the duty to inform can no longer be conceived as an obligation of textual deposit. When the platform operates under hypercuratorial anticipation, informing comes to mean making reconstructible, at the exact moment of decision, what the anticipatory curation itself tries to obscure. The mere existence of text is not enough. The essential content must be presented in a comparable, hierarchized, conspicuous and timely way. If the promotional architecture of the environment creates intensity and scarcity to hasten the decision, the duty to inform must work as a counterweight to this acceleration, and not as a bureaucratic ritual fulfilled in background documents. Likewise, advertising cannot be assessed only by its microscopic statement, because its capacity to deceive or abuse also depends on how it is inserted in the flow, what it highlights, what it omits, what equivalences it suggests and how it manages the perception of time, risk and loss.

The most important methodological consequence of this item is the following: consumer-law analysis must consider the communicational and decisional arrangement as a whole, and not only isolated fragments of its formal expression. The jurist must ask how the expectation was produced, when the relevant conditions were revealed, with what prominence they appeared, what the actual sequence between promise and acceptance was, and whether the consumer had real means to <1>p. 634</1> understand and compare what was being offered. This brings choice architecture back within the field of the CDC without technological mysticism and without creating a parallel law of platforms. It is simply a matter of recognizing that, when information, advertising and design operate together to govern the decision, legal control must also reach them in an integrated way<2><3>721</3></2>.

This shift prepares two operators. The first is open auditability, because, if abusiveness can reside in the communicational regime of supply, that regime must be institutionally reconstructible, with minimum preservation of screens, flows, messages, promotional pieces, interface changes and decision trails. The second is functional value equivalence, because the expectation produced by hypercuratorial anticipation cannot be dismissed as promotional smoke when it served precisely to induce the acquisition and shape the understanding of the object. If the platform promises a curated experience of value, rarity, performance or advantage, and later rebalances or downgrades it under opaque criteria, the frustration is not a mere annoyance. It may be a relevant inadequacy of the governed enjoyment itself.

In contexts under hypercuratorial anticipation, information, advertising and abusive practices belong to the same dogmatic problem. The platform does not merely offer an object; it organizes the semiotic field in which this object will be desired, understood and accepted. It is in this field that consumers learn what counts as an advantage, which losses they should fear, which costs they can ignore and which frustrations they should bear as normal. When this organization of meaning is conducted so as to displace what is essential, manipulate expectation and induce tolerance of loss under the appearance of freedom of choice, the CDC is not facing peripheral details of the digital experience. It is facing the very contemporary mode of exploiting vulnerability in IOCs.

The consumer-law discipline of the decision environment does not permit information, advertising and the formation of will to be artificially separated as if each of these dimensions operated in an isolated compartment. In the real process of consumption, especially in contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, these elements act together to shape the consumer's expectation, urgency, trust and practical disposition to adhere to and remain in the bond. The meaning of the transparency mandate can be traced back to the search for the “true and free will of the consumer”, functioning as a “precondition” for consumers to express their will freely and fulfill their legitimate expectations, that is, those that led them, “duly informed about the product or service, aware of their future contractual rights and duties”, to choose a given supplier as a contractual partner <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 818-819)</2>. This shows that transparency is not limited to the final instant of acceptance, but must characterize every pre-contractual manifestation of the supplier in the market. <3>↩</3>

In the consumer market, advertising and offer do not operate as watertight acts. Marketing communication takes part in manufacturing the very disposition to contract by stoking needs, organizing desires and at the same time presenting the path to their satisfaction, leading the consumer to the culminating moment of adhesion <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 91])</2>. For this reason, the legal reading of the decision process cannot artificially split advertising, information and contracting into autonomous compartments, as if each of these layers acted in isolation. This inseparability is heightened because the marketing message usually combines, in a single arrangement, concrete offers, fanciful promises and ancillary advantages integrated into a marketing mix, so that the social conduct of advertisers becomes a source of duties and obligations <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 95])</4>. In contexts under hypercuratorial anticipation, abusiveness is not located only in an isolated statement, but may emerge from the communicational regime of supply as a whole, that is, from the integrated way in which offer, persuasion and management of expectation are articulated to steer the consumer's decision. <5>↩</5>

Under the CDC, communicational unlawfulness is not restricted to frontal, conspicuous advertising that is easily identifiable as such. It can also arise in hybrid or disguised arrangements, or in ones embedded in apparently neutral media, in which the commercial message infiltrates narrative contexts that lower the consumer's critical vigilance and heighten their vulnerability to inducement <1>Pasqualotto</1><2>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 123-125])</2>. This occurs when marketing communication presents itself as entertainment, reporting or neutral recommendation, although in practice it works as a vehicle of commercial steering, which is why the outlet's responsibility lies precisely in not allowing advertising and editorial matter to be confused <3>Pasqualotto</3><4>(Pasqualotto, 1997, [p. 123-125])</4>. In these cases, the legal problem lies not only in the content conveyed but in the very blurring of the message's status. In contexts of hypercuratorial anticipation, abusiveness may result from the entire regime of inducement, and not only from a classic advertisement, above all when commercial communication dissolves into hybrid formats that confuse the consumer about the nature of what they see, read or follow. <5>↩</5>

The legal analysis of contractual and communicational mechanisms that affect the consumer's decision cannot be compartmentalized without seriously losing touch with the reality of the bond. Under the CDC, the consumer contract is not reduced to the final text of the pre-drafted clauses, because the consumer's will is formed over a relational process in which advertising, the information provided, commercial practices, ancillary promises and inducement techniques take a material part in building expectation and adhesion. Whoever interprets a consumer contract must observe not only the rule of Article 47 of the CDC, but all the provisions of the Code that establish the rights and duties of consumer and supplier, so that “the content of the contract to be interpreted is not only that ‘placed’ in clauses pre-drafted unilaterally by the supplier, but also the entire prior context that constitutes the offer”, such as advertising, brochures, information and commercial practices <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1015)</2>. This contextual interpretation also seeks the meaning of the contract in its negotiating context, treating prior acts and information as legally relevant and as part of the whole to be considered <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1030)</4>. Consequently, in environments under hypercuratorial anticipation, Consumer Law must examine the mechanisms of information, advertising and choice architecture together, since it is precisely from this integrated operation that the capture of expectation, the management of urgency and the exploitation of vulnerability may emerge. <5>↩</5>

Reconstructing the Consumer Protection Code as the normative infrastructure of the IOC regime requires, first of all, abandoning the reductionist reading according to which the CDC only works comfortably when the conflict involves a stable thing, one-off delivery and an obvious defect. This historical image helps explain the origin of many of the system's categories, but it does not exhaust its normative capacity. Brazilian consumer law already contains, in its own architecture, enough instruments to reach immaterial, continuous enjoyments governed by a third party, provided that its categories are read from the actual way the supply is performed, and not from nostalgia for a simpler, more tangible and far less complex market.

The point is neither to invent a new code nor to graft a foreign regime onto the legal text by force. The move is more disciplined and, for that very reason, stronger: bringing the CDC back to the type of conflict it now needs to control. In continuous digital services, the consumed object is not exhausted by its initial provision, because its enjoyment depends on maintenance, updating, curation, <1>enforcement</1>, informational processing and permanent modulation of the environment. In these cases, performance cannot be adequately understood as an instantaneous act followed by presumed stability. It takes place over time, through a managed relationship, and it is precisely this governed continuity that reshapes how quality defect, safety defect, adequate information, abusiveness, equivalence and performance are perceived.

This key also makes it possible to measure the inadequacy of conceptual responses that remain tied to static ontologies or to dramatically visible events of suppression. In platform ecosystems, legally relevant loss does not always appear as the abrupt disappearance of the object, because it is often produced by ordinary degradation, functional downgrading, informational obscuring, reclassification of access, unilateral changes to the conditions of use and progressive compression of the position of enjoyment.

The conflict no longer revolves only around the formal existence of the good or service and comes to involve the governance of the consumed experience. The reading of the CDC, in turn, must shift its focus from the contract as a statement to enjoyment as a relationship actually organized and controlled.

From this perspective, classic categories of the system gain new reach without having to be distorted. Product and service are no longer thought of only as media or isolated performances and come to be read in connection with the mode of enjoyment promised and managed. <1>p. 550</1> Vulnerability no longer operates only as an abstract premise of protection and comes to guide the identification of specific asymmetries produced by opacity, architecture, curation and regimes of proof. The duty to inform is not satisfied by the mere formal availability of data, because it must be reconstructed in terms of intelligibility and verifiability. Objective good faith no longer acts only as a clause of contractual courtesy and reappears as a technique for containing unilateral mutability and the unfair use of the supplier's position of control. The control of abusive practices, in turn, becomes particularly important because, on platforms, the exploitation of vulnerability is often built into the very design of the environment.

It is this shift that prepares the formulation of semiotic vulnerability as an operative category of the IOC. When enjoyment depends on signs, interfaces, metrics, histories, promises of progression and private criteria for recognizing the value consumed, consumer protection cannot remain blind to how the platform organizes meaning, expectation and proof. The CDC already offers enough language to confront this problem, provided one accepts that, in continuous digital consumption, to govern the environment is to govern enjoyment itself. And where enjoyment is governed, legal controllability cannot remain a prisoner of the contractual surface.

The aim is to show that the CDC can absorb the IOC regime without textual rupture, through a disciplined hermeneutic integration that is internally coherent with its protective matrix. It is to make workable <1>standards</1> suited to continuous digital consumption: informational adequacy understood as intelligible and verifiable information, minimum stability in long-lived objects, control of unilateral reconfigurations with functional and symbolic impact, and remedies compatible with managed mutability. Put simply, the goal is to strip the supplier of the privilege of calling “technical noise” what, seen with a little dogmatic honesty, is already a classic consumer-protection problem only now in new clothing.
